correctness.rationale: For every order d a de Bruijn Eulerian cycle provides p=2^d mutually different phase factors at all lengths at least d. The n-l+1 starts distribute modulo p with minimum floor((n-l+1)/p); every length d<=l<=L=floor((n-p+1)/(p+1)) has at least l+1 copies of each phase. This proves the p(L-d+1) lower bound. For n>=64, p=2^floor(log2(n/log2 n)/2) satisfies L>=d, p>sqrt(n/log2 n)/2, and p(d+1)<=sqrt(n log2 n), producing a deficit strictly less than 3sqrt(n log2 n). The published upper bound Phi<=n gives the limit. Independent direct counts for 15 constructions, 8 de Bruijn orders, and 20919 numeric cutoff cases matched; they are support, not infinite proof.

broader_coverage.reasoning: The closest stronger-looking numerical result uses an alphabet growing like sqrt(n), so its witnesses cannot be instantiated over binary for unbounded n. Encoding their distinct letters into binary blocks changes factor lengths and frequencies, and does not imply a saturation ratio of one. The present bound proves a different required quantifier: the alphabet is binary for every n.

originality.rationale: The central 2026 paper has the general upper bound Phi<=n and an asymptotically sharp witness on an alphabet with r distinct symbols for length r squared. Its proposition cannot specialize to binary for unbounded r. In the checked material the fixed-binary asymptotically saturated family and all-length explicit estimate were not established. The construction relies on the pair of properties unique de Bruijn phases and high periodic repetition counts, rather than the many-symbol period. Ordinary distinct-substring asymptotics and top-K frequent substring indexing use different statistics. Priority is qualified by unindexed literature risk.

value.rationale: A tightness example requiring a growing alphabet leaves open whether indexing over a fixed two-symbol alphabet can improve the leading worst-case n allowance. Constructing n-o(n) qualifying factors with binary symbols rules out any fixed-factor improvement solely from alphabet cardinality. The result supplies all-length explicit witnesses and verifiable factor-count cutoffs; it does not rely on a general downstream theorem or claim an optimal second-order deficit.
